title: Two accounts, conserved, and what the theorem says
objective: Read a conservation proof for what it uses, judge English restatements of what a theorem proves, and give an "if weakened" witness that refutes the claim's own proposition.

blocks.md: A proof that Lean accepts is only as useful as the statement it proves. Before you prove anything in the lab, practise reading a statement: what it covers, what it leaves out, and what happens when you weaken an assumption. Two questions to start; guess if you are unsure, because the point is to notice what you expect.

choice.prompt: `theorem transfer_conserves (s : Ledger) (n : Int) : total (transfer s n) = total s`. For which `n` does it promise anything?

options.text: Every integer, allowed or not
options.why: The statement has no hypothesis about `n`, and both branches of `transfer` conserve the total.

options.text: Only amounts the guard allows
options.why: The guard lives inside `transfer`, not in the statement.

options.text: Only `n ≥ 0`
options.why: Nothing in the statement restricts `n`.

options.text: Only when the transfer succeeds
options.why: A rejected transfer returns `s`, which keeps the total trivially, so the statement covers it too.

choice.prompt: Delete the guard from `transfer`. Which theorem stops being provable?

options.text: Conservation: the total is unchanged
options.why: (a − n) + (b + n) equals a + b for every `n`, as Z3 showed in S1 {{run:RUN-z3-conservation-noguard}}.

options.text: Non-negativity: both balances stay at zero or above
options.why: With a = 0 and n = 1 the sender ends at −1, and 1 is the minimal such amount {{run:RUN-z3-optimize-min}}.

options.text: Both
options.why: Conservation survives the loss of the guard.

options.text: Neither
options.why: Non-negativity needs `n ≤ s.a`, which is the guard.

blocks.md:
A theorem statement is a promise about every value of its variables. Read what stands before the colon: `(s : Ledger) (n : Int)` means "for every ledger and every integer". What the theorem promises depends on those variables and on any hypothesis written there, and on nothing else. `transfer_conserves` has no hypothesis about `n`, so it covers amounts the guard rejects too. For those, `transfer` returns the state unchanged, and an unchanged state keeps the total.

You will prove `transfer_conserves` yourself in LAB-2.2. Here is a proof of its parallel theorem, the same statement about `transferPos`, which also rejects a zero amount. Read it for what it uses, and watch for the guard.
The proof of `transferPos_conserves`, read for what it uses.
blocks.direction: Replay shows: the proof of `transferPos_conserves`, one tactic at a time. Look at what each branch receives, and at what each one uses.

code.text:
structure Ledger where
  a : Int
  b : Int
deriving Repr, DecidableEq

def total (s : Ledger) : Int := s.a + s.b

def transferPos (s : Ledger) (n : Int) : Ledger :=
  if 0 < n ∧ n ≤ s.a then { a := s.a - n, b := s.b + n } else s

theorem transferPos_conserves (s : Ledger) (n : Int) :
    total (transferPos s n) = total s := by
  unfold transferPos total
  split <;> simp <;> omega

call.prompt: Before `split` is shown: will any branch of this proof use the guard as a hypothesis?

options.text: The allowed branch
options.why: It receives the guard, but its goal holds for every `n`, so the guard goes unused.

options.text: The rejected branch
options.why: That branch returns `s`, and `s.a + s.b = s.a + s.b` needs no hypothesis.

options.text: Neither
options.why: Both branches conserve the total whatever the guard says. The guard shapes what `transferPos` does, not whether the total survives.

blocks.after: Neither branch needed the guard. In the allowed branch `s.a - n + (s.b + n)` equals `s.a + s.b` for every `n`, so the guard is in scope and unused. The proof lists only `propext` and `Quot.sound` as axioms, the two axioms of Lean's own logic {{run:RUN-lean-s2-cells}}.

choice.prompt: `transferAny s n` is `if n ≤ s.a then { a := s.a - n, b := s.b + n } else s`: a guard with no sign check. To prove `total (transferAny s n) = total s` you start with `unfold transferAny total` and `split`. What do the two goals look like?

options.text: Both goals have the guard `n ≤ s.a` as a hypothesis
options.why: Only the first branch has the guard. The second has its negation.

options.text: One goal, with the `if` removed and no new hypothesis
options.why: `split` produces a goal for each branch.

options.text: No goals, because `split` has proved the total unchanged
options.why: `split` divides the work and proves nothing.

options.text: Two goals: with `n ≤ s.a` in scope the debited and credited fields add up to `s.a + s.b`, and with `¬(n ≤ s.a)` in scope the goal is `s.a + s.b = s.a + s.b`
options.why: Each branch gets its own condition, and the rejected branch is the untouched state.

blocks.md: Now remove the guard and see what each proof really depended on. In the cell, `noGuard` is `transfer` with no `if` at all: it always moves `n`. Two theorems are tried, one per property, with the same tactic script for both.

blocks.direction: Replay shows: Lean's verdict on each theorem, with the guard removed from the transfer.

code.text:
def noGuard (s : Ledger) (n : Int) : Ledger :=
  { a := s.a - n, b := s.b + n }

theorem noGuard_conserves (s : Ledger) (n : Int) :
    total (noGuard s n) = total s := by
  unfold noGuard total
  simp <;> omega

theorem noGuard_nonneg (s : Ledger) (n : Int) (ha : 0 ≤ s.a) (hb : 0 ≤ s.b) :
    0 ≤ (noGuard s n).a ∧ 0 ≤ (noGuard s n).b := by
  unfold noGuard
  simp <;> omega

call.prompt: With no guard, does the conservation theorem still build?

options.text: Yes
options.why: Conservation is about the arithmetic of both fields, and (a − n) + (b + n) is a + b for every `n`. This is specimen SP-2.2.

options.text: No
options.why: The guard protects signs, not sums.

blocks.after: Conservation builds and non-negativity does not: Lean reports a possible counterexample for the second {{run:RUN-lean-noguard}}. With an amount of 1 and a sender at 0, the sender ends at −1, and Z3 found the same smallest amount in S1 {{run:RUN-z3-optimize-min}}. The guard protects signs, not sums.

choice.prompt: Which of these says exactly what `transfer_conserves` proves, no more and no less?

options.text: For every ledger and every amount the guard allows, the total after a transfer equals the total before.
options.why: This promises less. The theorem also covers the amounts the guard rejects.

options.text: For every ledger and every amount, neither balance goes below zero after a transfer.
options.why: That is non-negativity, another theorem. Conservation says nothing about signs.

options.text: For every ledger and every amount, the total after a transfer equals the total before.
options.why: It keeps every hypothesis and adds none.

options.text: For every ledger there is an amount for which the total after a transfer equals the total before.
options.why: "For some amount" is a far weaker promise, and an amount of 0 already satisfies it. The theorem says every amount.

blocks.md:
A claim card says what you proved and what would break it. Its "if weakened" field asks for a counterexample when an assumption is weakened, which is the roadmap's third rule. The witness has to refute this claim, not its neighbor: a witness for non-negativity does nothing for conservation.

Below is a demo card for CL-2.1, the claim about `transfer_conserves`. Its method, tool and version come from the LAB-2.1 receipt, and its "if weakened" field already holds a witness: drop `n ≤ s.a`, and a sender at 0 sends 1. Before the check runs, decide whether claim validation accepts the card.

blocks.direction: Check shows: `statespace check` validating this card against the claim rules on your Bench. On a phone you see the recorded result, labeled with its run.

code.text:
claim: CL-2.1
proposition: transfer_conserves, for every ledger and every amount
assumptions: sender and recipient are two distinct fields
model: the pinned challenge
method: lake comparator, from your LAB-2.1 receipt
correspondence: none yet
if weakened: drop n ≤ s.a; a = 0, b = 0, n = 1 leaves the sender at -1
requirement: a transfer never creates or destroys money

call.prompt: Will claim validation accept this card?

options.text: Accepted
options.why: With no guard conservation still holds, so this witness refutes CL-2.2, not CL-2.1.

options.text: Rejected: the witness does not refute this card's proposition
options.why: Claim validation requires the witness to refute the card's own proposition under the weakened assumption.

options.text: Rejected: the witness is not minimal
options.why: Minimality is not required, and an amount of 1 is minimal anyway.

blocks.after: The witness is real, but it belongs to the neighbor: it breaks non-negativity (CL-2.2), not conservation {{run:RUN-z3-optimize-min}}. For CL-2.1, weaken something that conservation actually uses. The next question gives you candidates.

choice.prompt: Which entry is a witness that refutes CL-2.1's proposition, `total (transfer s n) = total s`, under its weakened assumption?

options.text: Drop `n ≤ s.a`: a = 0, b = 0 and n = 1 leave the sender at −1.
options.why: That breaks non-negativity (CL-2.2). The total is still 0.

options.text: Let sender and recipient be one account, with both new balances computed from the old state: a self-transfer of 1.
options.why: The account's balance changes, so the total does {{run:RUN-z3-selftransfer}}.

options.text: Drop `0 ≤ n`: n = −5.
options.why: Money moves backwards and the total is unchanged.

options.text: One account, with the credit read after the debit: 10 transferring 5 to itself.
options.why: Reading after the debit is the fixed order, and the balance stays 10 {{run:RUN-lean-selftransfer}}.

choice.prompt: Which of these says exactly what `transfer_rejected` proves? Its statement is `theorem transfer_rejected (s : Ledger) (n : Int) (h : ¬ (0 ≤ n ∧ n ≤ s.a)) : transfer s n = s`.

options.text: For every ledger and every amount, the transfer returns the ledger unchanged.
options.why: This drops the hypothesis `h`. An allowed transfer does change the ledger.

options.text: For every ledger there is an amount the guard rejects, and the transfer leaves the ledger unchanged for it.
options.why: "For some amount" promises less than every amount.

options.text: For every ledger and every amount the guard rejects, no balance goes negative.
options.why: That is another property. This theorem says nothing about signs.

options.text: For every ledger and every amount the guard rejects, the transfer returns the ledger unchanged.
options.why: It names the hypothesis and the conclusion, and adds nothing.

choice.prompt: The goal is `(0 ≤ n ∧ n ≤ s.a) → n ≤ s.a`. After `intro h`, what do you have?

options.text: One goal, still `(0 ≤ n ∧ n ≤ s.a) → n ≤ s.a`
options.why: `intro` moves the left side of the arrow into scope, so the goal shrinks.

options.text: Two goals, `0 ≤ n` and `n ≤ s.a`
options.why: Splitting a conjunction is the job of `constructor`. `intro` names a hypothesis.

options.text: One goal, `n ≤ s.a`, with `h : 0 ≤ n ∧ n ≤ s.a` in scope
options.why: A proof of an implication takes evidence in and gives evidence out. `intro` names the evidence you are handed.

options.text: No goals
options.why: `intro` names a hypothesis and proves nothing.

blocks.title: Comparator Live
blocks.md: Comparator Live, a public site that checks Lean solutions against challenge statements, identifies each trusted challenge by `sha256(challenge.trimRight() + "\n")` and flags the untrusted ones as unreliable. Your receipts hash a challenge the same way. The pins are {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}. Two questions to trace: does `statespace hash` on your challenge equal the receipt's `challengeSha` and the published hash? Who wrote the statement you proved?

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: *Theorem Proving in Lean 4*, section 4.1 "The Universal Quantifier" and section 4.4 "The Existential Quantifier" (read 2026-10-24): what a statement over every `s` and `n` promises, and why "for some amount" promises less. https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/

A pin is the commit a ref pointed to when ls-remote read it; read_at is that instant. The record is stale 60 days after its started_at and is refreshed by re-running the commands in argv.

git ls-remote was first run with several ref patterns per command (HEAD plus refs/tags/... or refs/heads/...); for leanprover/lean4 and postgres/postgres that printed nothing with exit 0. The recorded run uses one pattern per command; the pin for lean4 tags and PR 14577 uses a trailing * pattern, and every matching ref is kept in refs.

refs/pull/14577/merge is not advertised; only refs/pull/14577/head is. The v4.35.0 tag points at eb6cafb7290e8bd5f2937522d8d804f58f02bafc, the commit the bench image's Lean prints in its version string.

Twin cards that name no git repository are not pinned here: Stripe's "Idempotent requests" API page, the Zanzibar paper (USENIX ATC 2019), Jepsen's PostgreSQL 12.3 analysis, the arXiv papers on Cedar and CCF, SymCert (FMCAD 2026) and the AWS Automated Reasoning checks pages. Each card states its own read date.
Isabelle is developed in Mercurial; the pin is from its GitHub mirror, isabelle-prover/mirror-isabelle.
input sha256 for each command is the SHA-256 of the lines it printed, joined by newlines with a trailing newline.
